name: @blobatar/react-native
description: React Native and Expo adapter for blobatar. Deterministic geometric avatars.
//sideEffects: No `*.css` entry, unlike every other adapter. Those carry one so a bundler cannot drop `import "blobatar/motion.css"`; there is no motion layer on this platform and no stylesheet to protect, so the field would be guarding nothing.

scripts.//prepack: See the same note in `packages/react/package.json`. It matters more here than anywhere: this package's first release cannot go out through `release.yml` at all, because npm will not register a trusted publisher for a name that does not exist yet, so its very first publish is a manual one, which is precisely the run with no turbo ordering in front of it.

//peerDependencies: `blobatar` is pinned to an exact major for the reason `packages/react/package.json` spells out: under ADR-0008 the major names the generation, so a mixed pair is the wrong picture rather than a version skew, and `packages/harness` asserts the range rather than trusting release tooling with it. The three React Native peers are the opposite case and take ranges: `react-native-svg`'s majors are its own, not blobatar's generations, so a caret is correct there. The floors are the New Architecture's, which is the only architecture current React Native has, and a lower floor would be a configuration nobody here can test and everybody would be asked to support.
//peerDependenciesMeta: Reanimated and worklets are optional because only `@blobatar/react-native/animated` imports them. A consumer drawing still or morphing blobatars installs neither, which is the whole reason the idle layer sits behind a subpath rather than at the package root. They are a pair rather than one dependency: Reanimated 4 moved worklets into their own package, and the Babel plugin that compiles them lives in the second one. The ranges are deliberately wide and are NOT what actually decides whether an install works: `react-native-worklets` ships a JavaScript half and a native half that must match exactly, and on Expo the native half is whatever the SDK compiled into the app binary. A version this manifest happily accepts still throws `Mismatch between JavaScript part and native part` at runtime. `npx expo install` is what resolves that for a consumer, and no peer range can.
//devDependencies: `react-native` is pinned to the exact version Expo SDK 54 ships, and the pin is not cosmetic: `apps/example-native` declares that version, and a floating range here resolves higher, hoists over it, and hands Metro a React Native whose internals do not match the one the app was built against. The peer range above stays open, because a consumer's React Native is their business. Both are here for types only and never load: `SvgProps` extends `ViewProps`, so `react-native-svg`'s declarations reach into `react-native` and `tsc` needs it on disk, but that package's own entry point is Flow-typed source Bun cannot parse, which is why `packages/harness` renders this adapter through a stub rather than the real components. `react` is deliberately NOT pinned the same way: it is a single version across the whole workspace, and forcing it down here drags every other app with it while `react-dom` stays put, which React itself rejects at runtime. The duplicate-React hazard that pin was trying to solve belongs to the example app and is solved in its `metro.config.js`.
//worklets-pin: `react-native-worklets` is pinned to the exact version Expo SDK 54 bundles, and it is a pin rather than a range for two reasons. This package *compiles* its worklets at publish time with that package's Babel plugin, so the compiler should be the oldest supported version rather than the newest; and `apps/example-native` runs against the SDK's native half, which is 0.5.1 exactly. A floating range here resolved to 0.6.1 and the app threw `Mismatch between JavaScript part and native part of Worklets (0.6.1 vs 0.5.1)` on the first render. The peer range above stays open, because a consumer's SDK is their business.
author: Alain
//check: No `bun run build` here. The build is a turbo task that `check` depends on, so it runs once for the whole workspace before any check reads a `dist`. A check that rebuilt its own package would delete `dist` out from under a concurrent check in another one.
